parts:
Hi Mateo,
Reducing the windowsizes for non-wear detection should help to detect the shorter non-wear periods, e.g.  to 30 minutes  and 30 minutes or even less.
Note that the non-wear detection method is primarily designed to detect large windows of monitor non-wear. It is not expected to work great for very short non-wear periods. The assumption I made was that those really short non-wear periods are both not common and also have a negligible influence on the overall sleep and physical activity estimates because of their short duration.

Further worth noting is that g.part3 argument 'ignorenonwear' enables you to decide what happens with detected non-wear periods.
If TRUE (default) these are not classified as rest/sleep, but as daytime inactivity. If FALSE then these non-wear periods are likely to be classified as rest/sleep.
Vincent


On Tue, 18 Dec 2018 at 18:50, Matteo Sattler <matteo....@gmail.com> wrote:
Dear Vincent!
Dear group members!

We have serious troubles when classyfing non-wear periods. Non-wear periods of up to 3 hours are often classyfied as rest/sleep periods via the angle algorithm. Interestingly, these periods are not detected and reported either in part2 (no angle alg. applied so far) nor part5.
I know that this can happen when the non-wear periods are very short but it also happens for periods of 2 hours (see example attached). We used both 60min and 30min windows for the non-wear detection, but the results were quite similar.

Did you ever experience the same problem and found a solution for it?


Many thanks!
Matteo
